A few scholarly publications reference the term, but few align with the concept of ChaaS we observe in the industry. Many refer to ChaaS as any instance of publicly accessible charging stations16,17,18 whereas others have employed the term to describe mobile charging “delivery” by means of large battery packs loaded on vehicles19,20. Singh et al. identify some of the functions we observe in ChaaS, placing it in the context of other energy-related services21. “X- as-a-service” (XaaS) was originally associated with various functions provided in cloud computing, including communication-as-a-service (CaaS), infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), and software-as-a-service (SaaS)22. Over time, the XaaS term has been invoked to refer to offerings outside the specific realm of computing. Examples include lighting-as-a-service, in which a provider covers the up-front cost of energy efficient lighting fixtures that a client pays to use over time, and mobility-as-a-service, which unifies and facilitates access to shared travel resources23. We observe the common thread unifying XaaS frameworks to be the offloading of asset ownership responsibilities in exchange for paid access to those assets over time. Accessing these assets “as a service” is typically the direct alternative to owning those assets, and the “as-a-service” modifier indicates a deviation from an ownership model status quo. In an analogy to cloud computing, the asset provided “as-a-service” would otherwise be owned by its users in the dominant ownership model. Most of the ChaaS models discussed in literature (“h” added to avoid confusion with CaaS models such as Containers-, Content-, and Communication-as-a-Service) describe vehicle charging provision models that do not align with that definition and are not direct alternatives to owning EVSE. For example, although public charging stations may provide charging to EV owners who do not own EVSE, their primary purpose is not to offload the responsibility of EVSE ownership from consumers to station operators. Instead, charging stations serve a variety of purposes, including vehicle range extension and provision of fast charging, which are more likely to supplement owned charging assets than replace them. In a second example, the functions of “charging delivery,” including responding to emergencies and providing convenience where charging is unavailable nearby, are unlikely to change vehicle operators’ equipment ownership responsibilities.
